source.title: The Break-Even Point on Optimization Trajectories of Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Stanislaw Jastrzebski; Maciej Szymczak; Stanislav Fort; Devansh Arpit; J. Tabor; Kyunghyun Cho; Krzysztof J. Geras

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies SGD learning rate and batch size and measures loss-surface geometry and gradient covariance along training trajectories, properties related to generalization in some claim versions. It does not directly measure the training–test generalization gap described by the claim.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own measurements of gradient covariance, Hessian, and batch-normalized network metrics. Validation accuracy is shown in figures, but it is not reported as a result on the claim versions; cited findings about generalization are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own training and validation accuracy curves for different SGD batch sizes under common epoch budgets: SimpleCNN and ResNet-32 on CIFAR-10 and LSTM on IMDB (Appendix E, Figures 11, 13, 15). These bear on V5 without requiring a training–test gap calculation. However, the supplied text does not preserve the plotted trajectories sufficiently to determine the direction of the held-out performance differences. The extracted geometry measurements do not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct: the authors present theoretical and empirical evidence that early SGD hyperparameters control subsequent gradient-covariance and loss-surface geometry, and leave connecting these observations to generalization for future work. That stated research boundary does not erase the relevance of their own batch-size validation curves to V5.
record.recipe_differences: Studies early-phase SGD learning-rate and batch-size effects on gradient covariance and Hessian geometry; it does not test the claim's training–test generalization outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate and batch size change measured covariance and Hessian properties. In SimpleCNN-BN, the smallest tested batch size is an exception for some metrics; a high learning rate is reported as necessary for improved conditioning relative to a network without BN.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger learning rates or smaller training batches reduce maximum covariance and Hessian spectral norms and generally improve covariance conditioning along SGD trajectories.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early SGD hyperparameters control gradient noise and loss-surface geometry after a break-even point.

fits_no_version.finding: The conditioning benefits attributed to batch normalization depend on learning rate in the tested SimpleCNN comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch normalization alone does not ensure favorable loss-surface conditioning at low learning rates.

record.problems: The study explicitly leaves a closer investigation of the Hessian and links to generalization for future work. Several outcomes are presented in figures; uncertainty estimates are not reported for the extracted comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No separately stated numerical outcomes for the remaining architectures, learning rates, or batch sizes are included as rows because the paper presents them in figures without text values; figures remain locators for the qualitative descriptions. Validation-accuracy curves in the appendix are not extracted because they do not report the training–test error gap in a way that tests these claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the corresponding natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
Width beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.

Closing a batch-size penalty through longer training, learning-rate scaling with warmup, or normalization and regularization changes. The direction and magnitude of the basic batch-size comparisons cannot be recovered from the supplied plot text.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and its ranking against norm and margin measures.
Removing memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

missing.what: Rows comparing validation accuracy across training batch sizes at matched epochs for SimpleCNN and ResNet-32 on CIFAR-10 and LSTM on IMDB. Although rows_left_out declares these curves omitted, its justification is incorrect: V5 concerns held-out performance and does not require calculating a training–test gap. The supplied text lacks readable trajectories, so no directional verdict can be assigned.
missing.locator: Appendix D training budgets and batch-sweep recipes; Appendix E, Figures 11, 13, and 15

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are justified from the readable results supplied. All eight extracted rows concern geometry rather than a version's named outcome. The batch-size validation curves make the study relevant to V5, but their values and ordering cannot be inferred from axis labels or from the geometry results.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization, natural-label test performance, and training–test error gap.
Network width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification test error.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and held-out performance.
Large-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training–test generalization gap.
Effect of removing memorized training examples on test accuracy.
